1:
Chrysostom marks a new stage: having shown from the Priest, the Priesthood and the Covenant that the old dispensation was to have an end, the writer now shows it from the fashion of the tabernacle itself. Chrysostom reads the two rooms as two periods, the holy place a symbol of the former, where all things are done by sacrifices, and the Holy of Holies of the present, by which he means Heaven, and by the veil the Flesh, since we enter within the veil through the veil of His flesh. His weight falls on the tense: the first had ordinances, so that even while the tabernacle still stood it already was not. Gill sets out the same design more plainly, that the chapter proves Christ's pre-eminence from the tabernacle as the preceding chapters proved it from the priesthood and the covenant; he adds that the word rendered ordinances signifies righteousnesses, so called because appointed by a righteous God, by which men became externally and typically righteous.

On the missing noun the voices are unanimous across every school, which is rare. Clarke observes that the translators supplied covenant as though the word stood in the apostle's mind, and that although several manuscripts of no good note read tabernacle, the best uncials with the Syriac, Ethiopic, Armenian and Vulgate omit it, so the reading is in all probability spurious. Ellicott agrees that since all ancient manuscripts omit the word and covenant has been the leading thought through a long succession of verses, the Authorised rendering is certainly correct. Robertson notes simply that there is no word for covenant in the Greek. Calvin is sharpest: he suspects an unlearned reader who could find no noun for the adjective supplied tabernacle himself, and records that it is absent from many of the best manuscripts and dismissed by Griesbach and all modern critics.

Over the worldly sanctuary they divide. Clarke stands alone in refusing the pejorative sense, holding that the apostle speaks in praise of a sublimely emblematic service and that the adjective properly means adorned, embellished, splendid, citing Pliny that the Greeks named the universe from its absolute elegance. Ellicott takes it the other way, that both place and ministrations belonged to this world and so stand in contrast with the heavenly things of which the Tabernacle was a token and shadow. Calvin holds both halves at once: the sanctuary in itself was earthly and rightly classed among the elements of the world, yet heavenly as to what it signified, since an effigy is a different thing from the reality. Robertson adds the grammar, that the adjective is late and stands in the predicate position, not the attributive. Henry presses the plainest sense, that it was wholly of this world as to its materials and a building that must be taken down.

The furniture divides them again, over how far it should be read. Henry allegorises freely: the tabernacle was a moving temple shadowing the unsettled state of the church militant, the lamps burned because there were no windows, which was to convince the Jews of the darkness of that dispensation, and the table stood opposite the candlestick to show that only by light from Christ can we have communion with him. Wesley agrees that candlestick and bread typified the light and life more largely dispensed by him who is the Light of the world and the Bread of life. Barnes is deliberately restrained and says so: though the writer maintains the whole institution was a figure and names every article, he never explains their particular typical character nor affirms that they had one. Calvin likewise abstains from any refined explanation. Clarke and Robertson keep to the fabric, the lamps lit at evening and put out at morning, the twelve loaves in two piles of six renewed each sabbath, and the shewbread a hendiadys for the table with the loaves of God's Presence.
3:
The second veil is named without explanation, and the voices supply different first ones. Barnes and Ellicott take the first to be the hanging for the door of the tent, so that the inner curtain, on which the cherubim were curiously wrought, is the second by way of distinction. Clarke makes the first the curtain that shut the holy place off from the court, keeping the people and even the Levites from seeing in. Gill objects that Scripture speaks of only one veil, and that there was one only in the tabernacle and in Solomon's temple, but that in the second temple, under which the apostle lived, two hung between the holy place and the holy of holies, renewed every year, and the innermost is meant. Barnes explains the room's name from the Shekinah dwelling between the cherubim; Ellicott observes that Holy of Holies renders a Hebrew idiom which does not itself occur in the Bible, made familiar through the Latin, and that the Temple descriptions use a different word.

Then comes the chapter's hardest verse. Ellicott says plainly that hardly any passage in the Epistle has given rise to more controversy, and that it bears on the question of authorship; the Greek word admits either censer or altar of incense, as both sides concede. He weighs the evidence evenly: the word is absent from the Pentateuch and occurs twice only in later books, both times for censer, while in Philo and Josephus it regularly means the incense altar, commonly called the golden altar though only overlaid with gold. Robertson sets out the same balance and refuses to resolve it, noting that one great manuscript places the clause in the previous verse, and leaving the discrepancy unsettled, since the incense altar was at any rate used for the Holy of Holies by its ritual associations.

The others take the censer and set about the difficulty of its location. Gill identifies it as the golden one used by the high priest on the day of atonement, silver serving on other days, and grants that Moses does not call it golden though Josephus does; he records that the Ethiopic version moved the clause up to the second verse to escape the problem, and refuses that expedient. Wesley says only that it was used by the high priest on the great day. Barnes answers at length: the writer described the sanctuary as it stood in his own time, Moses' silence proves nothing, the high priest was commanded to carry incense in a censer before the mercy seat, everything used there was of gold, and a vessel needed once a year would naturally be laid up in the one safe place. Clarke cuts the knot with Calmet: the apostle describes the Mosaic tabernacle, not Solomon's temple with its solid wall and wooden doors in place of the veil, so the passages need not be reconciled at all.

Over the cherubim the division is about restraint. Gill gathers the Jewish opinion, that they were two as at Eden, that Philo and Josephus called them winged fowls, that most rabbis took them for angels, and that Jerome derived the name from a multitude of knowledge. Wesley reports the supposition that each had four faces and so figured the Three-One God with the manhood assumed by the Second Person, and Clarke fills the space with a father's saying that Christ is himself Tabernacle, Table, Ark, Candlestick and both Altars. Barnes will have none of it, judging much of what is written here the mere creation of fancy, the design nowhere explained in Scripture, and silence the wiser course. Calvin approves the apostle for cutting off refinements unsuitable to his purpose and warns that to philosophise beyond just limits is not only useless but dangerous. Robertson keeps to the words, that the mercy seat here is the place and not the propitiatory gift of Romans 3:25.
6:
The description turns into a routine that carries the argument. Barnes and Clarke fill out the daily round of the outer room, incense at the morning and evening sacrifice, the lamps dressed, the shewbread renewed, the blood of the sin offerings sprinkled before the veil, work needing constant access; Wesley lists the same offices. Ellicott makes the observation that governs the paragraph: the present tense runs through these verses not because the writer thinks the services still continue, but because he is tracing the ordinance of Scripture, and describes the Tabernacle alone, since what he said of the ark would have been untrue of the temple of his own day, whose Most Holy Place stood empty. Calvin draws the conclusion the writer is driving at, that while the tabernacle stood the sanctuary was shut, so that only by its removal could the way to God be opened; the very form of the building told the Jews to look for something else, and those who kept the shadows obstructed their own way.

Once every year means one day, and every voice that counts the entries counts more than one. Ellicott notes that Leviticus prescribes two, with the incense and the bullock's blood, then with the blood of bullock and goat, while the Talmudic tract Joma makes four by splitting the first ministration and adding a return to fetch out the censer. Gill gives the same four and adds that a fifth made the high priest worthy of death, correcting Philo for saying a third or fourth was already fatal. Barnes reports three or four and holds the number immaterial beside the one point that matters, that this room was entered on one day and the other every day.

The word rendered errors opens a real division. Clarke takes it strictly, as transgressions of which the people were not conscious, made likely by the many ritual niceties through which a man might incur guilt unawares; he adds that the priest, clothed with infirmity himself, needed an interest in the same sacrifice, by which the nation understood itself absolved from the past year's errors and restored to access. Wesley states the restriction baldly, that these were sins of ignorance, to which only those atonements extended. Calvin denies the restriction: the Apostle does not mean mere ignorance but includes voluntary sins, for no sin is free of error, since however knowingly a man sins he is blinded by lust and cannot judge rightly, men never deliberately rushing headlong into ruin. Barnes agrees that the term passes from involuntary error to fault in general. Robertson grants that the papyri and inscriptions distinguish errors from crimes, yet insists that these sins of ignorance were sins and called for atonement.

The last verse names the teacher. Gill draws a chain of doctrine from the phrase, that the Holy Ghost existed under the Old Testament, that a personal act ascribed to him proves him a distinct person and truly God, that the Levitical ordinances were therefore of God and carried a spiritual meaning, and the saints of that age had some knowledge of it, which he authored. Barnes adds that the Spirit taught sometimes by revelation, sometimes by the written word, and here by symbol. Henry presses the application: these records are of use to Christians, who should not stop at reading the institutes of the law but learn what the Spirit signifies by them; the way to heaven was not so clear or so frequented then, God having since opened a wider door. Ellicott insists the sanctuary meant is the heavenly one, and adds that the contrast between priests and people scarcely appears in this Epistle, the only contrast being between the one High Priest and all who approach through him. Robertson sets the two veils side by side: the outer kept the people from the first tent, the inner kept the priests from the Presence.
9:
The word rendered figure is the ordinary word for parable, and Barnes insists on the difference: not the word for type, but one meaning a placing side by side, so that the service represented realities yet to be revealed. Clarke calls it a dark enigmatical representation, Gill a dark saying full of obscurity. Gill disputes the phrase that follows, preferring a figure lasting until the present time, that is until Christ came, over the Vulgate's figure of the present time. Ellicott renders it a parable unto the season that stands near it, and he, Robertson and Clarke all note the variant by which the following clause depends on the parable rather than on the time. Calvin takes the word as equivalent to antitype, explaining it by a portrait so like the man that seeing it reminds us at once of him, and adds that the present tense is a concession, the writer speaking as though he were one of those still sacrificing.

What the system could not do is stated flatly. Clarke observes that a man who brought his offering lawfully was exempted from many legal disabilities, yet even he who did the service best continued imperfect, with a guilty conscience and an unholy heart, since the blood of bulls and goats could not take guilt away. Calvin marks the contrast of flesh and conscience: the rites did not reach the soul to confer true holiness. Robertson calls this the real failure of animal sacrifice, at best a ritual purification calling for endless repetition. Barnes, having granted the service typical in general, warns against spiritualising every minute arrangement: safety lies in keeping close to the explanations the inspired writers supply, since an interpreter who takes leave of those pilots is on an open sea, to be driven he knows not whither.

The catalogue that follows is read as deliberately trivial. Gill points to the clean and unclean meats and the drinks forbidden to priests and Nazarites; Barnes takes the washings for the ablutions served by laver and brazen sea. Ellicott and Robertson agree that the best text drops the connecting word, so that carnal ordinances describes the gifts and sacrifices themselves, ranking those powerless offerings with the rules about food. Clarke enters a protest, that the word carnal is not used here, nor scarcely anywhere in the New Testament, in the degrading sense many preachers take the liberty of giving it; it means what pertains to the body. On the time of reformation he glosses the time of rectifying, when the ceremonial law was fulfilled and abrogated, the moral law more strictly enjoined, and spiritual worship taught. Robertson notes the noun is medical, used by Hippocrates of straightening misshapen limbs. Calvin hears behind it Jeremiah 31:31, the new covenant succeeding the old as a reformation, and says the trifling observances are named so that we may measure how far the Law fell short. Wesley compresses the whole clause into three words: till Christ came.

Then the sentence turns. Robertson calls it the crux of history, Christ coming on the scene and all being changed, and notes that the manuscripts divide between good things to come and good things already come, both true. Gill argues that he is come from the cessation of Jewish civil government, the destruction of the second temple, the expiry of Daniel's weeks, and the calling of the Gentiles. Henry founds all good things past, present and to come on that priestly office. Cyril quotes the whole passage in a lecture on the garden where Christ was crucified, to seal the cry It is finished: the mystery is fulfilled and sins are forgiven. Clarke thinks the verses badly divided and insists they be construed as one sentence. On the greater tabernacle they part: Wesley makes it his own body, Robertson heaven itself, and Calvin joins the two, Christ entering heaven through the temple of his body.
12:
Robertson states the distinction that governs the argument: other high priests offer blood, this one his own, so that he is at once victim and priest; the worth of the offering rests on his being Son of God as well as Son of man, sinless and so needing no offering for himself, and giving himself voluntarily. Barnes ranks the differences: the offering was wholly for others where the Jewish priest offered for himself too, it was his own blood, and it had real efficacy where the other was an emblem. Clarke fastens on the adverb, once for all against the annual entering, and glosses eternal redemption as a ransom price standing good for ever, endless in merit and efficacy. Gill adds that Christ was not of Aaron's order and that God would accept those sacrifices no longer. Calvin presses the alternative: if Christ's blood is reckoned no better than the blood of beasts, what expiation did his death make? Once he had come with its efficacious power, the typical observances had to cease.

The lesser term is the red heifer of the nineteenth of Numbers, and Ellicott recounts the rite, the spotless heifer wholly burnt with cedar-wood, hyssop and scarlet, the ashes laid up outside the camp and mixed with running water to sprinkle whoever had been defiled by the dead; the high priest was himself sprinkled twice in his week of preparation, lest he had been defiled unawares. Barnes notices its purpose, a standing sacrifice always at hand, sparing the expense and delay of a fresh offering whenever uncleanness arose. Wesley says it removed legal uncleanness and readmitted men to temple and congregation, Clarke that it answered the law's end, removing disabilities with the body in view. Calvin protests against stopping there. Many go astray, he says, by forgetting that sacraments are in question; to explain the cleansing of the flesh of what avails among men is heathenish, and wrong is done to God's promises if their effect is confined to civil matters, since Moses repeatedly declares iniquity expiated by a sacrifice duly offered. The blood of beasts was a true symbol, cleansing sacramentally, and the argument runs from sign to thing signified.

Then the phrase over which they divide most sharply. Barnes lays out four standing opinions: the third person of the Trinity, the divine nature of Christ, endless life as against perishable sacrifices, or the glorified person of the Saviour; he notes too that some manuscripts read holy for eternal. Clarke will not choose, taking it of the Holy Ghost, by whom Christ was conceived, wrought miracles and was raised, and of the eternal Deity dwelling in the man Christ Jesus which made his humanity's offering infinitely meritorious, since neither can well be considered apart from the other. Ellicott presses the article, an eternal Spirit rather than the, and denies that the Holy Spirit reference has any foundation in New Testament usage or in the context; the explanation must be sought in our Lord's own nature, comparing the spirit of holiness of Romans 1:4. Robertson agrees: this is Christ's own spirit, eternal as he is, giving his blood a moral quality no other sacrifice had. Calvin and Wesley go the other way, Calvin because a sacrifice meant for eternal expiation was a work more than human, so that the death Christ suffered as man becomes saving by the Spirit's power, and Wesley because redemption is the work of the whole Trinity.

The effect is stated in the same breath. Robertson catches the emphasis by pausing before the noun, dead not bodies but works; Wesley expands it to the inward and outward works of the devil, springing from spiritual death in the soul and leading to death everlasting; the service replacing them is the life of faith in perfect love. What the earlier rites never reached, Robertson adds, is exactly this: the conscience, not the flesh.
15:
One Greek word carries the verse, and the voices split over how to render it. Clarke says there was no proper reason to give testament here when almost everywhere else the translators give covenant, which is the proper sense; covenant must be retained, and few readers, he adds, are satisfied with the rendering of the verses that follow. Ellicott is equally firm: whatever be thought of the verses following, testament has no place in this one, since the preceding chapter's leading thought was a new covenant and the old has already been named three times here. Barnes gives the reason in a sentence: a will needs no mediator. Robertson and Wesley render covenant without argument.

The other side is not weaker, only older. Chrysostom takes testament and builds on it, and explains why the illustration was needed: the weaker sort were likely to distrust the promises precisely because he had died, so the writer turns that death into the ground of confidence, a testament taking force only when its maker is dead. He then works the analogy through. A testament makes some heirs and leaves others disinherited, which he hears in the prayer that they may be where he is and in the praying not for all but for those who believe through the apostles' word. It binds the legatees as well as enriching them, so after promises past counting he demands a new commandment; and it needs witnesses, whom Christ names, himself, the Father who sent him, the Comforter, and the twelve. Henry states the distinction that makes the reading possible: a covenant is an agreement between parties about things in their own power, a testament the voluntary deed of one person, duly executed and witnessed, bestowing legacies and taking effect only at his death.

On the office Clarke supplies the old usage, that the mediator witnessed the contract, slew the victim and sprinkled both parties with its blood; Barnes has him standing between God and man at variance. Calvin will not let the title be shared: the writer does not claim the honour for Christ in such a way that others may remain mediators alongside him, but holds all others repudiated when Christ took the office, and since he entered it only through death intervening, true of no one else, he alone can justly be deemed Mediator. Henry adds the two ends for which he holds it, to redeem men from transgressions that made them debtors and prisoners, and to qualify the effectually called for the promised inheritance.

The clause about transgressions under the first covenant is taken by all as looking backward. Robertson calls it a definite statement that the typical sacrifices drew their value from the cross, so that Christ's death is the basis of salvation for all saved before it and since. Clarke says the death had respect to all the time before it as well as after, to the conclusion of the world; Wesley, that the article of Christ's death divides the old covenant from the new. Barnes explains how earlier worshippers were saved: they offered blood which could not expiate, but offered it in faith, relying on promised mercy and looking to a perfect sacrifice. Calvin compares the retrospective effect asserted in Romans 3:25, corrects the tense so that the called are those already called, glosses receiving the promise as enjoying its fulfilment, and asks who could rest in a law so weak that its own remedies never accomplished what they represented. Gill sets the clause both ways, back to the purging of the conscience and forward to the inheritance. Ellicott alone distinguishes two things in the one death: measured against the penalty it is a ransom, a payment in place of a debt due, and when debt and payment become sin and punishment the ransom gives place to the sin offering, whose principle is death deserved and vicariously suffered.
16:
These two verses are the chapter's sharpest crux, and Ellicott states both cases before deciding. If the word means testament, he says, the Authorised rendering gives the sense well, and most hold that a new thought enters here: having spoken of a promised inheritance that cannot be valid unless death takes place, the writer turns to a second and common meaning of his leading word, the less strained because what passes between God and man is never exactly a compact between equals. Two arguments carry that reading: the maxim of the first verse makes no intelligible sense of a covenant but is easy of a will, and the phrase in the second, literally over the dead, is used of men and not of slain animals. Ellicott grants the case would be strong if the verses stood alone and were written of Gentile rather than Jewish usage; but he judges its difficulties worse than those it removes, since almost everywhere in the New Testament the sense must be covenant, and high authorities must treat these two verses as the single exception.

Barnes reaches the same place by counting. He tallies the thirty-three New Testament occurrences, then turns to the Septuagint, where the word stands nearly three hundred times and in more than two hundred translates the Hebrew for covenant; honest and inspired writers, he argues, would not take up a word in common use that failed to convey what the older writers meant by it. Robertson refuses to choose and finds the ambiguity deliberate, the same word carrying covenant in one verse and will in the next, a play he finds in Paul at Galatians 3:15; we ourselves say the New Testament rather than the New Covenant, and both terms are pertinent.

The disputed phrase is where the argument is really won or lost. Clarke prints a friend's rendering, that where there is a covenant the death of the appointed victim must be exhibited, since a covenant is confirmed over dead victims and is not valid while the appointed victim lives; the disputed participle, his friend observes, is not a noun, and the Greek has no word for testator or for men, so a substantive must be supplied, and the victim set apart for ratifying is the natural one. Clarke reports Wakefield rendering it almost identically, and concludes that we should forget testament and testator were ever introduced, since they totally change the meaning. Barnes meets the counter-objection, that the word for dead means only dead men and no Jew offered a human victim. The word men, he answers, is not in the Greek; there is no evidence that either language kept separate words for dead men, dead animals and dead vegetables; and this Epistle has used the same adjective of dead works, another writer of a dead lion.

The rest make their own peace with it. Calvin says the verse alone proves the Epistle was not composed in Hebrew, the Hebrew word meaning covenant and never testament while the Greek carries both; the writer alludes to the secondary sense but rests his weight on the thing itself. To the objection that God made no will with Israel but a covenant, he answers that the covenant bore a likeness to a will because it was ratified by blood, God adopting no symbol unnecessarily; and to the objection that the heathen also ratified covenants by sacrifice, that they borrowed the rite and not he. Wesley will not have the ambiguity exploited at all, thinking it beneath the apostle's dignity to play on a Greek word as the common translation supposes, and says of the next verse, with unusual candour, that neither rendering is literal and the passage is very perplexed. Gill alone takes the will without misgiving and expounds it, a testament of many gifts and legacies, with Father, Son and Spirit for witnesses and the blood of Christ for seal.
18:
Barnes treats this verse as settling the two before it. If the writer had just laid down that a will is not binding until its maker dies, how could that be a reason for ratifying a covenant with blood? He sees no connection; but grant that in covenant transactions with God the death of a victim is required, and everything follows. Calvin reaches the same result differently, insisting it is the fact and not the word that is urged: God's covenant might be called a testimony without impropriety, since angels, prophets, apostles and many martyrs have borne witness to it and the Son of God became its surety, though the Hebrew word will not mean covenant at all. No scrupulous regard, he concludes, is owed a word when nothing is advanced but what agrees with the thing.

The account of the ratifying raises a harder problem, Moses recording only part of it. Barnes states it squarely: nothing there of the blood of calves and goats, of water and scarlet wool, of sprinkling the book or the tabernacle; so the writer had it by tradition or by revelation. He argues for tradition, since fresh revelation would have wrecked an argument that depends on stating only what the Hebrews already granted. Robertson says the old narrative is used with characteristic freedom, that mingling water with blood and sprinkling with a wisp of wool had become customary, and that the writer passes over the oil, applying blood to every detail. Ellicott collects the missing particulars from elsewhere in the Pentateuch, the water keeping the blood from coagulating and increasing the purifying fluid, the scarlet wool perhaps binding the hyssop to a cedar stick. Wesley says the circumstances were known already from other passages of Moses, and guesses the water may also typify the blood and water of John 19:34.

On the book Clarke breaks with the rest. The sprinkling of it never took place: the words and the book itself belong grammatically to the verb of taking, not of sprinkling, so that Moses took blood, water, wool and book, and sprinkled the people. He describes the rite: blood caught in basins and mixed with water, a bunch of hyssop bound with scarlet thread, the sprinkling falling on those nearest, who stood for the rest, there being never blood enough for the whole congregation. Robertson allows only that Exodus is silent, though it may well have been done. Gill insists that what Moses spoke was the written law, audibly and in a known tongue, not the rabbis' oral law. Cyril takes the verse elsewhere altogether, as evidence that grace comes by water: heaven and earth are from the waters, the Spirit moved on their face before the six days, Israel was delivered through the sea, and where a covenant is made there is water also, with Noah after the flood and at Sinai with wool and hyssop.

Calvin makes the recital of the precepts the point of the next verse: a sign is an appendage to the word, no symbol was added before the Law was explained, that word was not whispered like a magic incantation but pronounced clearly for the people, and sacraments are perverted where the commandment goes unexplained. Barnes fastens on the verb enjoined: one party to a compact does not command the other, so God never surrenders his right to enjoin. Clarke hears our Lord quoting the same words at the supper, proof to him that his own blood was what the blood at Sinai meant. On the tabernacle Ellicott falls back on Josephus, who reports it sprinkled with blood as well as anointed with oil, and infers as much from the consecration recorded in Leviticus. Wesley says only that it was done yearly; Clarke draws the lesson, that all a sinner handles is polluted and nothing acceptable to a holy God without the sprinkling of atoning blood.
22:
The qualifying word draws attention. Ellicott says the Greek means rather that one may almost lay down the rule, governing both halves of the verse; Robertson agrees it qualifies the whole clause, not merely the subject. Gill reports and rejects a reading joining it to the verb instead, as though all were purged by blood but only almost perfectly. The exceptions are cleansings by water and fire, and Ellicott adds the provision letting the very poor bring flour for a sin offering. Calvin will not let even these stand outside: water drew its cleansing power from the sacrifices, and the purifying of metal and clothing carried no remission; and the people were never each sprinkled, so little blood being unable to reach so great a multitude, yet the purgation reached all. He also names Chrysostom and rejects his account of the word, which made it mark the unfitness of merely figurative rites. On the second clause Clarke shows the maxim was already rabbinic, there being no expiation but by blood, and explains the logic: the sinner has forfeited his life, and the victim's blood, which is its life, is shed in substitution, Christ giving human life for human life, dignified infinitely by union with God. Barnes presses further, that sin never has been and never will be forgiven except in virtue of shed blood.

Then the sentence that troubles everyone: the heavenly things themselves needed cleansing. Robertson admits it seems strained to speak of a ritual dedication of heaven by Christ's appearing, and calls the picture highly mystical. Barnes answers that the word does not imply heaven was unholy before, only that it is now accessible to sinners, as the earthly tabernacle was consecrated so that men might approach. Ellicott says the same more exactly: the heavenly things are not defiled by sin, but the true sanctuary cannot be entered until they are brought into association with the one atoning sacrifice.

The rest look elsewhere for the thing cleansed. Clarke sets down three opinions: heaven itself, set apart for the souls redeemed by that blood; the body of Christ, purified by its own sacrifice as he sanctifies himself in John 17:19; or the Church, to be presented without spot. Calvin objects that reading them as things in the sky has forced commentators to alter the sense of purified, and holds that the tabernacle represented Christ's whole kingdom, court and sanctuary for his work on earth and the holiest for his kingdom above. Henry takes them as the privileges of the gospel state, begun in grace and perfected in glory, and observes that the earthly sanctuary is a pattern of heaven, communion there being a heaven upon earth. Wesley reads them as our heaven-born spirits, adding with unusual frankness that what more this may mean we do not yet know.

Chrysostom supplies the reason the verse was needed. The Jews prided themselves enormously on the temple, repeating that it was the temple of the Lord; nowhere on earth was such a building for costliness or beauty, with gold in its walls, and it was revered besides for being one, drawing men from Babylon and Ethiopia. So, he says, as against the sacrifices the writer set Christ's death, here against the temple he sets the whole heaven. Barnes notices what follows: Jesus, of Judah and not of Levi, never entered the temple proper but had access only to the courts, like any other Jew. Ellicott draws the contrast tighter: the high priest came before a mere symbol of the Presence, filled the place with incense before entering, and dared not delay his return by lengthening his prayer, lest he excite terror in Israel; this one is made manifest before the face of God. Clarke goes furthest: Christ appearing in his crucified body before the throne is a real offering to divine justice, continuing there in the constant act of being offered.
25:
The single offering is defended here, and a sharp disagreement surfaces. Gill takes the verse as proof of a finished satisfaction, and turns it against two parties: those who hold that Christ offers himself now in heaven, and those who offer his body daily. Clarke, naming no controversy, says almost what Gill condemns, that the sacrificial act keeps its efficacy because the crucified body is still an infinitely meritorious sacrifice before the throne. Ellicott sharpens what is denied: the offering in view is not the killing of the victim but the presentation of the blood within the veil. Calvin asks how a man can be a priest who offers no sacrifice, and answers that a priest need not sacrifice continually, since even the Law had appointed days; the one sacrifice is perpetual in effect, and the eternal priesthood rests on a virtue that never fails.

The next verse states the absurdity of the alternative; Robertson explains its ellipsis, a condition assumed untrue, so repetition would have required him to suffer often since the world began. Calvin declines to press that phrase, the world having been founded and ordered before sin entered; a popular way of speaking, intelligible to common readers though not suitable to over-nice and hair-splitting critics. Wesley states it best: the sacrifice divides the world's whole duration in two and extends its virtue backward and forward from the point where they meet. On what was put away they differ. Clarke takes it narrowly, as abolishing the sin offerings and ending the Mosaic economy, though he reports the other application to guilt and power in believers; Barnes takes both punishment and stain, and Robertson quotes the distinction that this sacrifice dealt with sin as a principle, the Levitical offerings with transgressions. Cyril, on the same appearing, warns that a manifestation in time is no beginning of being, the goings forth of the one manifested being from eternity.

The argument then rests on the common lot of men. Barnes finds its force in the oneness of the great events: men die once, are judged once, have one probation, so one sacrifice was fitting; and death is by appointment, neither chance nor a debt of nature. Gill agrees that it comes not from nature but from sin and God's decree, so a man's days can be neither lengthened nor shortened. The exceptions are handled alike: Gill and Clarke name Enoch and Elijah and those alive at the coming, Ellicott says a few passing twice through death does not touch the general law, Calvin restricts the saying to the ordinary lot. Wesley adds a careful denial: though every man's final state is fixed at the moment of death, there is not a word in scripture of a particular judgment immediately after it.

The last verse is built on that parallel, and Ellicott shows how exactly: the two halves answer point for point, with the first subordinated to the second. Over the many they divide. Gill denies that Christ bore the sins of all men, since all have not faith and are not justified; Wesley says as many as are born into the world; Calvin declines the question, the contrast being not between few and many but between many and one, since he died for others and not himself, though he grants that unbelief keeps many from the benefit. On the second appearing they are united. Robertson notes it is apart from sin, with no notion of a second chance, and that the waiting verb is used of looking for the Saviour in Philippians 3:20. Clarke glosses without sin as without a sin offering, takes the salvation to be the raising of believers' bodies, and breaks into prayer that the Lord would come. Calvin ends where he began: we need not be disquieted by longings for new expiations, since at that coming the one death's efficacy will be openly manifest.
